name: Beninese Amiwo (Pâte Rouge)
description: Amiwo, meaning 'fat pudding', is a beloved Beninese staple - real technique cooks the cornmeal directly in a blended tomato, onion, and chili sauce rather than as a plain porridge served alongside, which is what gives amiwo its real red color and deep flavor, distinguishing it from plain pâte (wo). Real versions are boldly seasoned with black pepper and chili, not lightly touched, and it's traditionally served with grilled chicken or fish and a fresh tomato-onion relish.

ingredients_full.note: standing in for the traditional Beninese chili, generous

ingredients.note: standing in for the traditional Beninese chili, generous

steps_detailed: Blend the tomatoes, onion, and jalapeño into a smooth puree.
Fry the puree with the garlic in the palm oil, 8-10 minutes, until it reduces and deepens.
Stir in the tomato paste and black pepper, being generous with the pepper.

Add 1.5 cups water and bring to a boil, then whisk in the cornmeal directly into this red liquid, stirring constantly, 15-18 minutes, until very thick and it pulls away from the sides of the pot - this real technique is what makes amiwo, not plain porridge served beside a sauce.

name: Beninese Wo (Corn Fufu)
description: Wo, a plain cornmeal paste, is Benin's everyday staple starch, traditionally served with sticky sauces like crin-crin or assrokouin to amplify its flavor.
steps_detailed: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.
Gradually beat in the remaining cornmeal, stirring vigorously, over medium-low heat 15-18 minutes, until very thick and smooth.
steps: Whisk about a third of the cornmeal with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.
Gradually beat in the remaining cornmeal, stirring vigorously, over medium-low heat 15-18 minutes, until very thick and smooth.

name: Beninese Poulet Braisé (Grilled Chicken)
description: Grilled chicken, real technique marinated boldly with generous garlic and pepper, is the classic accompaniment to amiwo.
steps_detailed: Marinate the chicken in the garlic, pepper, and lemon juice for at least 20 minutes, being generous with both the garlic and pepper.
Grill, turning, 12-15 minutes, until charred and cooked through.
steps: Marinate the chicken in the garlic, pepper, and lemon juice for at least 20 minutes, being generous with both the garlic and pepper.

name: Beninese Crin-Crin Style Stew
description: A sticky, mucilaginous vegetable stew in the spirit of crin-crin (jute leaves), real jute leaves aren't a distinct item here, so okra and spinach stand in for a similar sticky texture.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef, 6-7 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and simmer 6-8 minutes.
Add the okra and spinach, and simmer 10-12 minutes until the stew turns naturally sticky and thick.
steps: Brown the beef, 6-7 minutes.

name: Beninese Ablo
description: Ablo, a soft, slightly sweet steamed rice cake, is a beloved Beninese street food, real technique fermenting the batter for real tang before steaming.
steps_detailed: Blend the cooked rice with a little water and the sugar into a smooth batter.
Let ferment at room temperature 6-8 hours for real tang.
Steam in small portions over simmering water 15-18 minutes until set.

name: Beninese Riz au Gras
description: Riz au gras, a rich tomato-and-meat rice dish, is a common Beninese one-pot meal shared across the wider Francophone West African region.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion, 6-7 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and carrot, and simmer 10 minutes.
Stir in the rice and 1.25 cups water, cover, and simmer 18-20 minutes until tender.

name: Beninese Peanut Sauce
description: A rich groundnut sauce, real technique whisking the peanut butter slowly and generously seasoning with chili for real depth.
steps_detailed: Brown the chicken, 6-7 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter slowly with the tomatoes and jalapeño, being generous with the chili, and add to the pot.
Simmer 20-22 minutes until the chicken is tender.

name: Beninese Fried Fish
description: Fried fish rubbed generously with garlic and pepper, reflecting Benin's coastal fishing tradition along the Gulf of Guinea.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and pepper, being generous with both.
Fry in a little oil, 3-4 minutes per side, until golden and cooked through.

name: Beninese Fresh Tomato Onion Relish
description: A fresh tomato and onion relish, the real, traditional accompaniment to amiwo, meant to cut through its richness.
steps_detailed: Toss everything together just before serving.

name: Beninese Fried Plantain
description: Fried ripe plantain, a common Beninese side dish, real versions using genuinely ripe plantain for real caramelization.
steps_detailed: Fry the plantain slices in a little oil, turning once, 3-4 minutes per side, until deeply caramelized and golden.

name: Beninese Bean Fritters
description: Fried black-eyed pea fritters, closely related to Nigerian akara and shared across much of West Africa.

description: A simple, hearty beef and vegetable stew, common Beninese home cooking.
steps_detailed: Brown the beef with the onion, 8-9 minutes.
Add the carrot, potato, and tomatoes, and simmer 30-35 minutes until tender.

steps_detailed: Whisk the mayonnaise and mustard together.
Toss with the cabbage and carrot until well coated.

name: Beninese Bissap
description: Bissap, a hibiscus drink, is a beloved Beninese beverage shared across much of West Africa.
steps_detailed: Warm the hibiscus tea and stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Chill and serve over ice.
